description: Trip To The Trenches is a python based coding project with a unique and super fun objective, in this program the user pilots a submarine and descends through Earth's real ocean zone - from sunlit shallow waters to the blinding dark of the Mariana trench. Navigate, discover real marine species at every depth, and see how deep you dare to go! Anyone from beginners to pros everyone is welcome here 💗
summary:
Trip to the Trenches is a deep-sea dive simulator written in Python. The player pilots a submarine from the sunlit surface through five real ocean zones, from the Epipelagic to the Hadopelagic trenches, and meets 24 real marine creatures along the way. Each creature has a depth, danger level, bioluminescence setting and a fact, so players learn about deep-sea life by exploring it.

Players can descend and surface, search for any creature by name, and build a dive log sorted by depth, danger or zone. The game ends with a dive report showing the deepest zone reached, creatures discovered and a rank.

Under the hood, a linked list keeps the zones in order, a stack tracks the player's route, binary search finds creatures by name, and a hand-written selection sort orders the dive log.

Most of the deep ocean is still unexplored, and this project turns ocean science into something anyone can explore. It was built solo while learning Python and data structures, with final-stage development assisted by Claude (Anthropic).
details:
What it does and how it works: Trip to the Trenches is a terminal-based deep-sea dive simulator written in Python. The player pilots a submarine through five real ocean zones, from the sunlit Epipelagic zone down to the Hadopelagic trenches, and can descend, surface, and search for any of 24 real marine creatures by name. Each creature has a depth, a danger rating, a bioluminescence setting and a fact. Discovered creatures go into a dive log that can be sorted by depth, danger or zone, and the game ends with a dive report showing the deepest zone reached, creatures found, and a rank.

How it is built: A linked list keeps the zones in order, and a stack remembers the player's route, so descending pushes a zone and surfacing pops it. Binary search finds creatures by name in alphabetically sorted lists, and a hand-written selection sort orders the dive log. Two classes, Zone and Creatures, hold the data.

Benefits and impact: The project makes ocean science approachable. Players learn real animals, their depths and their adaptations, such as bioluminescence, by exploring instead of reading a list. Most of the deep ocean is still unexplored, and the game gives students a simple way to start getting curious about it.

Tools: Python 3, Visual Studio Code, Anaconda, and GitHub for the code repository. It runs on any laptop and needs no extra libraries.

Creativity: The game turns a data-structures project into a journey, with colors that change by zone, a typing effect, a depth meter and an ASCII submarine. Every creature is a real species.

Factors considered: Depths are approximate and the danger level is a game rating, not a scientific measure. I kept the design beginner-friendly, made each data structure do a real job in the game, and avoided external libraries so it runs anywhere. I built it solo while learning Python and data structures, and used Claude (Anthropic) to help with final-stage development.
